title: Reading for Speed, Backwards
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note describes an unconventional nonfiction reading technique: reading the conclusion first, then returning to the beginning armed with the knowledge of where the argument is headed. The logic is that knowing the destination makes it far easier to quickly identify which supporting arguments, examples, and stories actually matter, letting readers move through the body of a text faster without losing comprehension. The author is explicit that this only applies to nonfiction, and frames it as a tool for efficiency rather than pure speed.
points: A technique for nonfiction reading: read the ending first, then return to the beginning with that context.
Knowing the conclusion in advance makes it easier to spot which supporting arguments matter most.
This approach is framed as improving efficiency and comprehension, not simply increasing raw reading speed.
The technique is explicitly limited to nonfiction; using it on fiction is described as ruining the experience.
The piece positions this as one tool among several used by highly efficient, voracious readers.
quotes: Active learners are voracious readers who consume a tremendous amount of information from many sources.
Examine a learner who is not as focused on speed as on efficiency and superior comprehension and you are likely to see someone who does something very odd.
When a reader knows where the author is going, reading the supporting arguments can be accomplished much more quickly without sacrificing comprehension.
Speed is replaced by efficiency in this process and will enable readers to spend the time they believe is necessary to capture the critical ingredients of a book or essay.
when it comes to nonfiction, reading backward is a way to read more.
